newsitem.title: UK: NTT jumbo Euroyen bond sparks controversy.
newsitem.headline: NTT jumbo Euroyen bond sparks controversy.

text.p: Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) raised 100 billion yen ($886 million) on international capital markets on Tuesday in a highly controversial deal, bankers said.

The appointment of two U.S. banks to underwrite the deal has been seen as a serious snub by some Japanese securities houses in London, already struggling to save face after financial scandals in Japan.

On top of that, many banks involved in selling the bond said buying was limited because it was too expensive, although the underwriters Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley said they had met with strong demand.

"It is disgraceful from my point of view that NTT decided to give the mandate to Merrill and Morgan Stanley," a senior capital markets executive at a Japanese bank in London said. "This is an attempt by the American houses to move into the Euroyen market."

NTT's 100 billion yen 10-year bond is the first liquid Euroyen bond to come to the market this year and the first corporate to tap yen for many years. It was priced to yield four basis points over 194 JGBs. An official at Morgan Stanley said no political message was to be read in the mandate.
"The deal was given to us because we went to NTT with the idea in the first place," the official said.

"NTT based the mandate on the idea and the commitment to the transaction," he said, adding it would improve Morgan Stanley's competitive position in the sector to have underwritten a benchmark Euroyen bond.
Many banks involved in selling the deal said it offered too little yield pick-up over existing Euroyen paper to entice investors, but they expected the lead managers to support the price.
"The bond is too expensive, by between five or 10 basis points, but will not widen immediately because the leads are committed to keeping it at that level," a trader at a European bank said.
"They have to keep it there, partly because NTT has had so much attention," he said.

Other 10-year Euroyen bonds available include deals from the European Investment Bank and Japan Development Bank, both of which were trading around two b.p. through JGBs on Tuesday. Spain has a 10-year bond outstanding which offers around nine notches over the curve.
"There was some switching out of EIB and JDB paper, but the yield pick-up was not enough to entice many investors into corporate debt," a Euroyen trader at a Japanese bank said.
"Many funds are waiting for the bonds to widen a bit before they buy, because they are interested in buying a liquid, Euroyen issue," he said.
Officials at both Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley said there was strong buying of the bonds from British, European and Middle Eastern institutions, and said they had sold most of the paper already.
"Japan has one of the largest bond markets in the world but there has been no international issuance this year," a Merrill Lynch official said.

"There has been a demand and supply imbalance, and most secondary market paper has traded through the curve. This is providing a liquid transaction which is yielding above the curve for a triple-A name," he said.
Bankers said the pressure would be on the two U.S. houses to make sure the bond performed.
"This is a massive coup for them, there is no doubt," a dealer at a Japanese bank said.

"If the spread widens it will be a bit of an embarrassment, but not that much. With the various scandals and things going on, some of the Japanese houses are difficult to select as underwriters at the moment."
-- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7748 ($ = 112.9 Japanese Yen)
